title: I'm burned out at work
seoTitle: Burned Out at Work? What the Bible Says and What Helps
description: Exhausted in a way sleep doesn't fix? What burnout is, how it differs from depression, what the Bible says about work and rest, and steps for this week.
summary: When work has taken more than it should: rest, limits, and what work is actually for.
answer: You're tired in a way a weekend doesn't fix. You wake up already dreading the day, you've stopped caring about work you used to care about, and some days you wonder whether anything you do there matters at all. Many people call this burnout. It isn't laziness, and it isn't a failure of faith; it's what happens to a person who has carried too much for too long with nowhere to set it down. You don't have to solve it tonight. Start smaller: stop working at a set time, and put your phone somewhere other than your bedroom so you can sleep. Tomorrow, tell one person the truth about how tired you are. And if the heaviness has spread past work into nearly everything, see a doctor this week. If you've had thoughts of ending your life, call or text 988 now.
happening:
It doesn't feel like one bad week. It feels like months of running on something other than energy. You sleep and still wake up tired, and Sunday evening brings a knot in your stomach. You answer email at eleven at night because it's easier than lying awake thinking about it. Small requests feel enormous, and the part of you that once cared about doing the job well has gone quiet, replaced by a flat voice that asks *what's the point*. You may still be good at your job, which is one reason nobody notices, sometimes not even you.

Being tired and being burned out aren't the same. Tiredness is what a hard week leaves behind, and sleep and a real day off put it right. Burnout is the kind of tired they no longer reach. The World Health Organization's International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11) defines burnout as a syndrome resulting from chronic workplace stress that hasn't been successfully managed, with three marks: feelings of exhaustion, a growing mental distance from your job or cynicism about it, and reduced effectiveness at work. The WHO includes it as an occupational phenomenon and says it isn't classified as a medical condition. It also uses the term only for work, not for other areas of life.

That last point matters, because depression can look a lot like burnout, and it isn't confined to work. The National Institute of Mental Health describes depression's signs as lasting most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks. Fatigue is one of them, which is why the two get confused, but so are losing interest in things you used to enjoy, changes in sleep or appetite, and feelings of worthlessness or guilt. If a week off didn't touch it, or the flatness has followed you home, please see a doctor, and read [I feel empty, and I don't know why](/help/empty). Exhaustion that won't lift can have physical causes too, and a doctor can look for them.

Each common explanation gets something right. The medical one remembers that you're a body, and a body denied rest for months will stop cooperating. Psychology describes how stress with no end in sight wears a person down. The spiritual explanation is right that we can ask work to carry what only God can carry, though it's sometimes told in a way that only adds guilt. Taken alone, each leaves out the rest of you. You're one person, not three, so whatever helps will have to reach your body and your heart together, and it will mean an honest look at the job itself.

scripture.intro: Scripture doesn't pretend work is easy. It makes room for a man who lay awake over his work, calls work good while admitting that it hurts, and answers the slavery of Egypt with a day of rest. Then Jesus calls the weary to himself. Read together, these passages show a God who made us to work and made us to stop.

passages.text: So my heart began to despair over all the labor that I had done under the sun. ... For what does a man get for all the toil and striving with which he labors under the sun? Indeed, all his days are filled with grief, and his task is sorrowful; even at night, his mind does not rest. This too is futile.
passages.reading: By any outside measure, the Teacher of Ecclesiastes had succeeded. He built houses and planted vineyards, surpassed everyone in Jerusalem before him, and says his heart took delight in his work (Ecclesiastes 2:4-10). Then he looked at all of it and called it "a pursuit of the wind" (Ecclesiastes 2:11). What he describes here sounds very much like burnout, down to the mind that won't switch off at night. God kept these words in the Bible, so you don't have to pretend your work feels meaningful when it doesn't. But see where the Teacher goes next: "Nothing is better for a man than to eat and drink and enjoy his work. I have also seen that this is from the hand of God" (Ecclesiastes 2:24). Joy in work is a gift. Work can't produce it, and it can't carry the meaning of a life.

passages.text: And to Adam He said: “... cursed is the ground because of you; through toil you will eat of it all the days of your life. Both thorns and thistles it will yield for you, and you will eat the plants of the field. By the sweat of your brow you will eat your bread, until you return to the ground— because out of it were you taken. For dust you are, and to dust you shall return.”
passages.reading: Work came before the curse. God put the first man in the garden "to cultivate and keep it" (Genesis 2:15), so work belongs to what human beings were made for. What the fall changed for work was the ground: the work goes on, but now it runs through thorns and sweat, and it ends in dust. If a job that was supposed to feel like a calling feels like a fight, this is part of the Bible's answer. You work in a broken world, and some of what you feel is the thorns. That doesn't excuse a cruel workplace, but it should quiet the voice that treats your exhaustion as a verdict on your worth. And the thorns won't have the last word; Paul writes that creation will be "set free from its bondage to decay" (Romans 8:21).

passages.text: Six days you shall labor and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God, on which you must not do any work ... so that your manservant and maidservant may rest as you do. Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and that the LORD your God brought you out of there with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. That is why the LORD your God has commanded you to keep the Sabbath day.
passages.reading: The Ten Commandments appear twice in Scripture, and the Sabbath command gives a different reason each time. In Exodus it's creation: God made the world in six days and rested on the seventh (Exodus 20:11). Here it's the exodus: you were slaves, and God brought you out. Remember what that slavery was like. When Moses and Aaron asked Pharaoh to let the people go to worship, he stopped supplying straw, kept the brick quota the same, and told the foremen, "You are slackers!" (Exodus 5:17). The Sabbath answers Pharaoh's economy. A slave can't stop; a free person can. Notice too whom the command protects: children, servants, animals, and the foreigner, "so that your manservant and maidservant may rest as you do." If anyone works for you, this command is about their rest as well as yours.

passages.text: Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest. Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me; for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For My yoke is easy and My burden is light.
passages.reading: A yoke is a tool for work, so what Jesus offers the weary is a different master and a different way to carry the load, rather than a life with nothing to carry. Later in Matthew he says the scribes and Pharisees "tie up heavy, burdensome loads and lay them on men's shoulders" (Matthew 23:4); here the teacher is "gentle and humble in heart." Then look at the very next scene. On the Sabbath his hungry disciples pick grain, the Pharisees accuse them, and Jesus defends them with the prophet Hosea's words, "I desire mercy, not sacrifice" (Matthew 12:7). The rest he gives isn't one more performance to get right. It's mercy for tired, hungry people, and among the loads he lifts is the need to prove you're worth something.

whyHard:
The usual explanation for burnout is that we work too much, and some of that is true. Some jobs ask more than one person can give. But hours alone don't explain this kind of tired. The Bible was written among farmers, shepherds, and laborers whose work was hard and physical, and it doesn't pretend otherwise. What's changed isn't only how much we work. It's what we've asked work to do for us.

We've asked it to tell us who we are. *What do you do?* is one of the first questions we ask a stranger, and the answer can feel like a verdict on a person's worth. When work is where your worth gets decided, every mistake feels like a sentence and rest feels like losing ground. The philosopher Byung-Chul Han described this in *The Burnout Society*, first published in German in 2010. He argued that a society that once drove people with orders and prohibitions has become what he called an achievement society, which drives them with endless possibility. No one has to force us, because we force ourselves, and since the pressure feels like freedom, we exploit ourselves until we burn out. You don't have to be a Christian to recognize that, though Scripture had a picture for it long ago: Pharaoh needed taskmasters to drive his slaves, and we've learned to drive ourselves.

The phone made it harder. For many of us, work now rides in our pocket, and it follows us to dinner and to bed. Even when no message comes, part of your mind stays on duty all evening, listening for one. Ecclesiastes describes a man whose mind doesn't rest at night (Ecclesiastes 2:23). We've built a world that makes him normal.

And many people can't simply walk away. The rent is due, the health insurance comes through the job, and there are children to feed. When losing your job would put your family at risk, it's hard to say no to anything, and an employer who knows that holds more power than it should. Scripture doesn't blame the worker for that. The law that gave Israel its day of rest also told employers to pay a poor worker "each day before sunset, because he is poor and depends on them" (Deuteronomy 24:15), and the letter of James warns wealthy landowners that the wages they withheld "are crying out against you" (James 5:4). Some burnout grows from the need to prove ourselves, and some from a job that would wear anyone down. It can be both at once, and it helps to know which part is which.

The church should have been the one place that told the truth about this, and too often we've made it worse. We've praised the volunteer who never says no and the pastor who never takes a day off. We've preached that work matters to God, which is true, and said far less about rest, as if the God who hallowed the seventh day had nothing to say about ours. Those of us who work for churches can make overwork sound like devotion, since our work is about God, and I'm a pastor, so I'm not pointing at this from outside it. A church that runs on exhausted people teaches them, whatever the sermon says, that God wants their output more than he wants them.

Underneath all of it is an old question: what makes a person worth something? Our culture's answer, and too often the church's, is what you produce. The Bible answers before you've produced anything. In its opening account, human beings are made on the sixth day, and the next day is the one God rests on and makes holy (Genesis 1:31-2:3), so the first whole day they lived was a day of rest they hadn't earned. Work is good, and doing it well is one of the ways we love God and our neighbor. But no one can rest while still trying to earn the right to exist, and no job will ever tell you that you've earned it.

thisWeek.intro: You can't undo months of exhaustion in a week, and you don't have to. Start with the smallest thing here. If you're a pastor or work for a church, there's a word for you in the questions at the end of this page.

steps.title: Give today an end
steps.body: Pick a time to stop working tonight and keep it. Turn off work notifications, put your phone somewhere other than your bedroom, eat a real meal, and go to bed. When Elijah collapsed under a broom tree, God's first answer was food and sleep, then more of both (1 Kings 19:5-8), and a psalm says God "gives sleep to His beloved" (Psalm 127:2). Sleep is one way a creature trusts God to keep the world running without it.

steps.title: Tell one person the truth
steps.body: Choose someone you trust, a spouse, a friend, or a pastor, and say it plainly: *I'm more worn out than I've been letting on.* You don't need a plan or an explanation. It's easy to look fine while you're running out, and keeping up the look is its own kind of work. One honest sentence lets someone help carry what you've been carrying alone.

steps.title: Take one real day off
steps.body: Choose a day this week, or as much of one as your job allows, and stop: no work, no work email, no catching up. Worship, sleep, eat with people you love, walk outside. Christians disagree about how the Sabbath command applies now (see the questions below), but a day of rest in every seven is a gift worth receiving. If you work shifts or two jobs, start with a few protected hours. God first gave the Sabbath to people who had just been slaves (Exodus 16:29-30). It was never only for people with flexible schedules.

steps.title: Make a doctor's appointment
steps.body: Call your doctor this week, or a clinic if you don't have one. Say how long you've been exhausted, what's changed in your sleep, appetite, and mood, and whether it follows you outside of work. A doctor can check for physical causes and for depression, and can document what's happening if you need time off. Going is one way of caring for the body God gave you.

steps.title: Talk to your manager about the load
steps.body: Write down everything you're carrying, including the work nobody sees, and then ask for a conversation: *Here's what's on my plate. I can't keep doing all of it well. What can we drop, delay, or give to someone else?* When Moses judged the people alone from morning until evening, his father-in-law told him, "the task is too heavy for you. You cannot handle it alone," and helped him share it (Exodus 18:18). If raising this with your manager doesn't feel safe, start with human resources or a trusted colleague.

steps.title: Take an honest look at the job
steps.body: Once you've slept, make two columns: what the job itself demands, and what you've added, like hours no one asked for or the need to be indispensable. Then ask whether this is a hard season or a hard job, and whether your role, your hours, or eventually your workplace could change. Many people can't simply quit, and nobody should decide in their most exhausted week. If you're weighing a change, talk it through with someone wise, and read [How do I know what God wants me to do?](/help/decisions)

moreHelp.body:
Burnout becomes more than a pastoral matter when your body or mind starts to give way. If rest hasn't touched the exhaustion in weeks, if the heaviness has spread beyond work, or if you're relying on alcohol or anything else to get through, see a doctor. For drinking or drug use, SAMHSA's National Helpline, with the other lines at the end of this page, can also point you to treatment. I'm a pastor, not a physician, and nothing here is medical advice.

If a doctor finds that your health is affected, ask about medical leave. In the United States, the Family and Medical Leave Act gives eligible employees of covered employers unpaid, job-protected leave for a serious health condition that keeps them from doing their job, and some states have leave laws of their own. Whether any of it covers you depends on your employer and your situation; human resources can tell you, and an employment lawyer can help if there's a dispute. This is general information, not legal advice.

A counselor can help with what lies underneath, like why saying no feels impossible. Ask your doctor for a referral, check your insurance company's directory, or ask a pastor which counselors nearby they trust. If you want a Christian counselor, find one who is also licensed, and confirm the license with your state's licensing board. If you've had any thoughts of ending your life, don't wait for an appointment: call or text 988 now, or call 911 if you're in immediate danger.
signs: The exhaustion has lasted for weeks, and rest no longer touches it.
The heaviness has spread beyond work to nearly everything, most of the day, nearly every day, for two weeks or more.
Your sleep or appetite has changed a lot.
You're drinking more, or using something, to get through the week or to fall asleep.
You're not being paid what you're owed, or you're being punished for asking about leave. Talk to an employment lawyer.
You've had thoughts of ending your life, or that your family would be better off without you. Call or text 988 now.
moreHelp.firstCall: You don't need a speech. To a doctor you might say, *I've been exhausted for about three months, and rest isn't helping. It's starting to affect my work and my family.* Be honest about drinking and any medication; it helps them help you. If you may need time off, ask whether they can document what they find. With a counselor, ask whether they're licensed in your state, whether they take your insurance, and whether they're comfortable working with your faith.
moreHelp.cost: Cost shouldn't be the reason you wait. A visit to your regular doctor is often covered by insurance, and many employers offer an employee assistance program with a few free counseling sessions. Counselors may offer sliding-scale fees, and community mental health centers and university training clinics often charge less. Some churches keep a fund for needs like this. If money is part of the weight, start with [Money is a weight on me](/help/money).

helping.body:
If someone you love is burning out, you may see it before they'll admit it: a shorter temper, dread on Sunday night, the flat voice when work comes up. They may defend the job even while it wears them down, because admitting how tired they are can feel like failing. Skip the lecture about balance, and help with the load in ways they can accept: take something off their plate at home, guard their sleep, and don't become one more voice asking things of them this week. If it's your grown child, tell them what I want my five sons to hear from me: they were loved before they accomplished anything, and they still are.

If you manage people, you can do more than a friend can. Ask your people what they're carrying, protect their time off, and don't send the late-night message that makes rest impossible. The Sabbath was never only for the one in charge (Deuteronomy 5:14). If you serve on a church board, that includes your pastor.
say: You seem worn down. How are you, really?
What can I take off your plate this week?
You don't have to earn a day off with me.
Can I help you find a doctor?
You matter to me more than anything you get done.
dontSay: At least you have a job.
God won't give you more than you can handle.
helping.next: Check back in a week; one conversation won't lift months of exhaustion. Offer something concrete, like a ride to the doctor or an evening with the kids so they can sleep. If they're weighing whether to leave the job, help them think it through without deciding for them. And if the tiredness turns into hopelessness, or they talk about not wanting to be alive, ask them directly, *Are you thinking about suicide?* Stay with them, and call or text 988 together.

prayer:
Lord, I'm tired in a way sleep hasn't fixed. I get up and do it again, and some days I can't remember why. You know what this work has taken from me, and what I've handed it that it never asked for.

I've tried to earn my rest and to prove my worth by how much I can carry. Forgive me for treating myself like a machine and calling it faithfulness.

You gave Your people a day of rest when they came out of slavery. You gave Elijah bread and sleep before You gave him a word. Your Son took His tired friends away to rest, and He still calls the weary to come to Him. So I'm coming, as tired as I am.

Give me sleep, and the nerve to stop. Give me wisdom for the conversations I've been avoiding. If this work is Yours for me, teach me to carry it with You. If it isn't, show me, and give me courage when it's time to go.

I was Yours before I'd done anything. Teach me to rest like I believe it.

Amen.

faq.a: No. Exhaustion isn't a sin. Jesus grew tired (John 4:6) and slept through a storm (Mark 4:38), and he was "without sin" (Hebrews 4:15). Burnout can have sin tangled in it, though, ours and other people's. Sometimes we can't stop because we're trying to prove something, and sometimes an employer demands more than is right. Name each honestly. Confess what's yours, and set down what was never yours to carry.

faq.q: Is it wrong to hate my job?
faq.a: Hating a hard job isn't a sin in itself. The Teacher of Ecclesiastes wrote, "I hated all for which I had toiled under the sun" (Ecclesiastes 2:18), and the Bible kept his words. The letter to the Colossians told slaves, whose work wasn't theirs to choose, to work "for the Lord and not for men" (Colossians 3:23). That verse can be used to squeeze more out of tired people, but it gave the least honored workers a different audience, and the same letter told their masters to supply them with "what is right and fair" (Colossians 4:1). You can do honest work in a job you don't love, and still decide, in time, that it's the wrong job.

I can't tell you that, and nothing here is financial advice. Some jobs should be left: work that's dishonest, unsafe, or abusive, or that is slowly wrecking your health or your family. Others are hard seasons that could change with an honest conversation, a different role, or fewer hours. Try not to decide in your most exhausted week. Sleep, see a doctor, and talk to your manager if you can. Then decide with the people your choice will touch, your spouse above all, and with someone who can look clearly at your finances.

faq.q: Do Christians still have to keep the Sabbath?
faq.a: Faithful Christians answer this differently, and the historic creeds don't settle it. Some hold that the Sabbath command is part of God's moral law, rooted in creation (Exodus 20:11), and that it now falls on the Lord's Day, the first day of the week, when the early church gathered (Acts 20:7); to them a whole day given to worship and rest is both a gift and a protection. Others hold that Christ fulfilled the Sabbath, since Colossians counts it among things that are "a shadow of the things to come, but the body that casts it belongs to Christ" (Colossians 2:16-17); to them rest is found in a person, and every day belongs to him. Still others keep the seventh day itself, because the commandment names it (Exodus 20:10) and Jesus went to the synagogue on the Sabbath "as was His custom" (Luke 4:16); to them the day God made holy at creation (Genesis 2:3) is still a weekly appointment with him. All of them agree that rest is God's gift.

faq.q: How do I recover from burnout?
faq.a: Slowly, and by changing something as well as by resting. A week off helps, but if you return to the same load and the same need to prove yourself, you return to the same exhaustion. Start with your body: sleep, food, and a doctor's visit. Then look honestly at the load and talk with your manager. Then take up the harder question of why you couldn't stop, with a counselor or a friend who will tell you the truth. If weeks pass and nothing lifts, tell your doctor, and read [I feel empty, and I don't know why](/help/empty).

faq.q: I'm a pastor and I'm burned out. What should I do?
faq.a: Start where you'd tell anyone else to start: sleep, a doctor, and one honest conversation. Tell your elders or board the truth now, while it's still a conversation and not a crisis. Take your day off and your vacation, and let someone else preach. Find a pastor outside your church you can talk to freely, and a counselor if you need one. When the apostles came back from their mission with no time even to eat, Jesus said, "Come with Me privately to a solitary place, and let us rest for a while" (Mark 6:31). I'm a pastor too, so I'm writing this to myself as much as to you. The church belongs to Christ, and it will still be his on your day off. More for pastors is gathered at [I'm a pastor and I'm running on empty](/help?need=pastors).

slots.note: James was raised without a father and came to faith from atheism. If he wants it told, a few sentences in his own words on whether either shaped how he learned to tie work to worth would strengthen the paragraph on identity (the one that names Byung-Chul Han). The section stands without it.

The pastor's answer says only that James is a pastor writing to himself as much as to other pastors. He could add, in his own words, what rest actually looks like in his week, or a season when ministry wore him down. No story has been written for him.

Where James lands on whether and how Christians keep the Sabbath. The answer states three views (a Lord's Day Sabbath, the Sabbath fulfilled in Christ, the seventh day itself) with a verse and a comfort for each and lands on none; step three says only that Christians disagree. If he wants his own landing, it belongs in his words, in one place.
The line about his five sons is conviction only (what he wants them to hear from him). He could add, in his own words, how he talks with his sons about work and worth.

sources.claim: Burn-out is included in ICD-11 as an occupational phenomenon and is not classified as a medical condition. It is defined as a syndrome resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed, characterized by energy depletion or exhaustion, increased mental distance from one's job or negativism or cynicism related to it, and reduced professional efficacy, and it refers specifically to the occupational context.
sources.cite: World Health Organization, Burn-out an occupational phenomenon: International Classification of Diseases (news release, 28 May 2019); ICD-11 code QD85

sources.claim: Depression's symptoms last most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks; its signs include fatigue, loss of interest or pleasure in hobbies and activities, changes in sleep and appetite, and feelings of guilt or worthlessness.
sources.cite: National Institute of Mental Health, Depression

sources.claim: Byung-Chul Han argues that disciplinary society, governed by prohibition and obligation, has given way to an achievement society governed by an unlimited can, in which compulsion presents itself as freedom and the achievement-subject exploits itself until it burns out. First published in German in 2010. The page paraphrases the idea and quotes nothing.
sources.cite: Byung-Chul Han, Müdigkeitsgesellschaft (Berlin: Matthes & Seitz, 2010); English: The Burnout Society, trans. Erik Butler (Stanford Briefs, Stanford University Press, 2015)

sources.claim: The Family and Medical Leave Act entitles eligible employees of covered employers to unpaid, job-protected leave, including for their own serious health condition that makes them unable to perform the functions of their job; coverage depends on the employer and on the employee's eligibility.
sources.cite: U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division, Family and Medical Leave Act

sources.claim: Nothing in the FMLA supersedes a state or local law that provides greater family or medical leave rights, so state leave laws can apply as well.
sources.cite: 29 CFR 825.701, Interaction with State laws (Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School)

sources.claim: Asking someone directly whether they are thinking about suicide is recommended; asking does not cause or increase suicidal thoughts.
sources.cite: National Institute of Mental Health, Frequently Asked Questions About Suicide

reviewed.notes: Second editorial pass (2026-09-30) over the writer's pass. Truth: the WHO's ICD-11 wording was re-checked through search excerpts of the WHO release of 28 May 2019 (who.int is egress-blocked here), and the page now follows it as far as it goes: a syndrome resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed; feelings of exhaustion, mental distance from the job or cynicism about it, and reduced professional efficacy (it had said a sense of being no longer effective); included as an occupational phenomenon and not classified as a medical condition (it had said rather than a medical condition); the term kept to work, not other areas of life. The NIMH sentence now describes depression's signs as lasting most of the day, nearly every day, for two weeks, instead of calling depression symptoms. Byung-Chul Han re-checked against summaries of The Burnout Society (a disciplinary society of prohibition giving way to an achievement society of unlimited can; auto-exploitation attended by a feeling of freedom); the paraphrase is accurate and stays. The FMLA sentence stays general (eligible employees of covered employers; unpaid, job-protected leave for one's own serious health condition), now adds that state leave laws may also apply (29 CFR 825.701, added to sources), says coverage depends on the employer and the situation, and says plainly it is general information, not legal advice. Colossians is no longer attributed to Paul outright, in line with the Study Bible's authorship note (the letter to the Colossians; the same letter); Colossians 2:17 is now quoted as counting the Sabbath among the shadows, as its plural says; Genesis 1:31-2:3 is the Bible's opening account rather than its first chapter. Contested: the Sabbath answer now gives each of the three views two texts and a comfort of its own (the seventh-day view gains Exodus 20:10, Genesis 2:3, and what the day means to those who keep it; Luke 4:16 is quoted for what it says, synagogue on the Sabbath), with no landing; step three still says only that Christians disagree; the slot stands. Care: the answer now tells the midnight reader to call or text 988 for any thought of ending their life; the page's foot now shows 988, the Crisis Text Line, SAMHSA's helpline, and 911 (crisisTopics suicide and substance), so More help points drinking or drug use to SAMHSA's line there; burnout is told apart from tiredness and from depression and sent to a doctor and /help/empty without diagnosing. Voice: the knows, knows, knows anaphora in What's going on is broken up, and the way out will reach is softened to whatever helps will have to reach; each section keeps at most one Not X. Y. Kit: /plans/empty kept and relabeled as a plan for when you feel empty (its own subtitle; the plan names long exhaustion among the roots of emptiness); the other labels match their targets' titles. Flagged, not changed: /life/work-as-worship narrates James's own experience with his sons, and /writing/your-work-was-never-going-to-save-you and /writing/burnout-is-not-a-badge carry first-person confessions in his voice; the care page repeats none of it. Still to re-open at the source before release (egress-blocked here): who.int, nimh.nih.gov, dol.gov, and the Stanford and De Gruyter pages for Han. Validator clean; CarePage test run. Read again as the midnight reader, the skeptic, a pastor, and a licensed counselor.
